repairs.text: Strongest feature: Hernandez defines the soul as an immaterial substance containing consciousness and animating the body, then supplies two routes: consciousness is neither identical with nor reducible to the brain, and persons exceed brain and body. Principal limitation: This opening announces its decisive ontology without establishing it, because containing consciousness, substantiality, and bodily animation remain underspecified, with no independent warrant that the proposed entity exists or performs either function. Live burden: The later case must demonstrate that mental-physical differences require a substantial conscious bearer, rather than merely indicating incomplete physical explanation, contestable identity, or alternative descriptions of one embodied system. Locked score: Direct engagement with the motion, a lucid definition, and an organized two-part roadmap justify the locked score of 76, although existence and animation remain promissory.

Strongest feature: Hernandez gives a concise identity-based inference: beliefs can be true or false, whereas brain states as physical tissue are not truth-valued, so mind and brain differ in property and cannot be numerically identical. Principal limitation: The comparison leaves unanswered the physicalist reply, under which organized neural states realize representational content possessing truth conditions although their material vehicles, independently, are not literally true or false. Live burden: He must establish that truth-bearing content cannot be realized by, constituted through, or attributed to neural organization before this difference supports an immaterial bearer rather than distinct descriptions of one physical process. Locked score: Precision, central relevance, and an explicit conclusion justify the locked score of 74, while excluding physical representation and bridging nonidentity to a soul remain insufficiently defended.
